meta.title: Italian — Sounds and spelling
meta.subtitle: 23 letters, double consonants, stress and written accents — start here, beside CILS A1
meta.desc: How Italian is read, before or beside the first word: 23 notes, one card each — the five vowels, 11 consonant letters and groups of letters whose sound is not the English one (c, ch, g, ci and gi before another vowel, gli, gn, sc, qu, r, s, z), and 7 rules: the silent h, the doubled consonant, where the stress falls and when it is written, and the accents that tell la from là. The front shows the letters. The back gives, for each position the letters can stand in, the sound in the International Phonetic Alphabet and the English sound it resembles, then up to three words of the CILS A1 deck with a speaker beside each and the letters picked out; where the spelling does not decide the sound (an open or a close e, s between two vowels, z, the stress) the word's own transcription stands beside it. Say the word, then press the speaker and compare. Of CILS A1's 1004 words, 454 contain one of these spellings or a doubled consonant and 41 end in a written accent. THE ORDER is the vowels, the consonants in alphabetical order, then the rules. At the default of ten new cards a day the deck takes 3 days; it is meant to be studied beside CILS A1, not finished first. — WHAT IS NOT HERE: no description is written for this deck. Each English comparison is a cell of the first page named below, each context and rule a sentence of the second (two are from the third), with a cut marked […]. A row is carded only where a CILS A1 headword shows it, so gh has no card, and the letters that sound as an English speaker expects (b, d, f, l, m, n, p, t, v) have none. No source here says which syllable of every word is stressed, so the two stress cards give the rule and three transcribed words, and the stressed syllable is not marked on the other cards. The speaker is your device's Italian voice reading the example word, so a device without one is silent. — English comparisons: Wikipedia, “Help:IPA/Italian”, revision 1385545483 of 2026-11-13. Contexts and rules: Wikipedia, “Italian orthography”, revision 1385885869 of 2026-11-15; Wikipedia, “Italian phonology”, revision 1374139897 of 2026-09-10 (all CC BY-SA 4.0). Transcriptions: English Wiktionary, via kaikki.org (CC BY-SA 4.0). Example words and meanings: the CILS A1 deck on this shelf (English Wiktionary via kaikki.org, CC BY-SA 4.0).

fields.Says: Of those, only ⟨a⟩ represents one sound value, while all others have two.

fields.Says: In stressed syllables, ⟨e⟩ represents both open /ɛ/ and close /e/. […] There is typically no orthographic distinction between the open and close sounds represented, although accent marks are used in certain instances […]. In unstressed syllables, only the close variants occur.

fields.Says: In addition to representing the vowels /i/ and /u/, ⟨i⟩ and ⟨u⟩ also typically represent the semivowels /j/ and /w/, when unstressed and occurring before another vowel. Many exceptions exist […].

fields.Says: The letters ⟨c⟩ and ⟨g⟩ represent the plosives /k/ and /ɡ/ before ⟨h⟩ and before the vowels ⟨a⟩, ⟨o⟩, ⟨u⟩. They represent the affricates /tʃ/ and /dʒ/ when they precede a front vowel (⟨i⟩ or ⟨e⟩).

fields.Rows:
before a front vowel ⟨i⟩ or ⟨e⟩
/k/
scar
as in
chewhat
chiwho
perchébecause
fields.Says: When the "hard" (plosive) pronunciation /k/ or /ɡ/ occurs before a front vowel ⟨i⟩ or ⟨e⟩, digraphs ⟨ch⟩ and ⟨gh⟩ are used, so that ⟨che⟩ represents /ke/ or /kɛ/ and ⟨chi⟩ represents /ki/ or /kj/.

/ɡ/
again

/dʒ/
job
as in
buongiornogood day
il giornoday
giàalready
fields.Says: The letters ⟨c⟩ and ⟨g⟩ represent the plosives /k/ and /ɡ/ before ⟨h⟩ and before the vowels ⟨a⟩, ⟨o⟩, ⟨u⟩. They represent the affricates /tʃ/ and /dʒ/ when they precede a front vowel (⟨i⟩ or ⟨e⟩).

fields.Name: before another vowel
fields.Rows:
⟨ci⟩ […] before another vowel
/tʃ/
check
as in
ciao/ˈt͡ʃa.o/hello!
ciò/ˈt͡ʃɔ/this
⟨gi⟩ […] before another vowel
/dʒ/
job
as in
il giorno/ˈd͡ʒor.no/day
già/ˈd͡ʒa/already
fields.Says: The letter ⟨i⟩ can also function within digraphs (two letters representing one sound) ⟨ci⟩ and ⟨gi⟩ to indicate "soft" (affricate) /tʃ/ or /dʒ/ before another vowel. In these instances, the vowel following the digraph is stressed, and ⟨i⟩ represents no vowel sound: ciò (/tʃɔ/), giù (/dʒu/).

fields.Rows:
before ⟨i⟩ (before other vowels, the trigraph ⟨gli⟩ is used)
/ʎ/
billion
as in

fields.Says: ⟨g⟩ joins with ⟨l⟩ to form a digraph representing palatal /ʎ/ before ⟨i⟩ (before other vowels, the trigraph ⟨gli⟩ is used) […]. Between vowels these are pronounced phonetically long, as in /ˈaʎʎo/ aglio, "garlic" […].

/ɲ/

fields.Says: ⟨g⟩ joins […] with ⟨n⟩ to represent /ɲ/ with any vowel following. Between vowels these are pronounced phonetically long, as in […] /ˈoɲɲi/ ogni, "each".

fields.Rows:
before ⟨e⟩ and ⟨i⟩
/ʃ/
shoe
as in
uscireto go out
lasciareto leave
la sceltachoice
Otherwise
/sk/
as in
la scuolaschool
scoprireto uncover
il rischiorisk
fields.Says: The digraph ⟨sc⟩ is used before ⟨e⟩ and ⟨i⟩ to represent /ʃ/; before other vowels, ⟨sci⟩ is used for /ʃ/. Otherwise, ⟨sc⟩ represents /sk/, the ⟨c⟩ of which follows the normal orthographic rules explained above.

fields.Rows:
⟨qu⟩
/kw/

⟨cqu⟩
/kkw/

fields.Says: Normally /kw/ is represented by ⟨qu⟩, but it is represented by ⟨cu⟩ in some words, such as cuoco, cuoio, cuore, scuola, scuotere, and percuotere. […] The sequence /kkw/ is always spelled ⟨cqu⟩ (e.g. acqua) […].

/r/
trilled r
as in
buongiornogood day
buonaseragood evening
arrivedercigoodbye
fields.Says: Intervocalically, single /r/ is realised as a trill with one or two contacts. […] Geminate /rr/ manifests as a trill with three to seven contacts.

At the start of a word before a vowel […] or a voiceless consonant
/s/

between vowels
/s/ or /z/
as in
la casa/ˈka.sa/, /ˈka.za/house
la cosa/ˈkɔ.za/, /ˈkɔ.sa/thing
il bisogno/biˈzoɲ.ɲo/need
⟨ss⟩
/ss/
as in
permessomay I? (said to ask for permission)
essereto be
adessonow
fields.Says: It can be either voiceless or voiced (/s/ or /z/) between vowels; in standard Tuscany-based pronunciation some words are pronounced with /s/ between vowels (e.g. casa, cosa, così, mese […]), but most words are pronounced with /z/ (e.g. bisogno, rosa […]); in Northern Italy (and also increasingly in Tuscany) ⟨s⟩ between vowels is always pronounced with /z/ whereas in Southern Italy ⟨s⟩ between vowels is always pronounced /s/. ⟨ss⟩ always represents voiceless /ss/ […].

fields.Rows:
/ts/
cats
as in

il marzo/ˈmar.t͡so/March
il ragazzo/raˈɡat.t͡so/boy
/dz/
dads

fields.Says: ⟨z⟩ represents a dental affricate consonant; either /dz/ (zanzara /dzanˈdzara/) or /ts/ (canzone /kanˈtsone/), depending on context, although there are few minimal pairs. […] ⟨zz⟩ may represent either a voiceless alveolar affricate /tts/ or its voiced counterpart /ddz/ […].

fields.Name: h is never sounded
fields.Says: In addition to being used to indicate a hard ⟨c⟩ or ⟨g⟩ before front vowels (see above), ⟨h⟩ is used to distinguish ho, hai, ha, hanno (present indicative of avere, "to have") from o ("or"), ai ("to the", m. pl.), a ("to"), anno ("year"); since ⟨h⟩ is always silent, there is no difference in the pronunciation of such words.
fields.Pairs:
avere, "to have"the same sound
hoo ("or")
haiai ("to the", m. pl.)
haa ("to")
hannoanno ("year")
fields.Examples:
as in
avereto have
oor
l'anno/ˈan.no/year

fields.Name: a doubled letter is a longer sound
fields.Says: Except /z/, all consonants after a vowel and before /r/, /l/, a vowel or a semivowel may be geminated. Gemination in IPA is represented by doubling the consonant (fatto [ˈfatto], mezzo [ˈmɛddzo]), and can usually be told from orthography.
fields.Examples:
as in
il fatto/ˈfat.to/fact
tutto/ˈtut.to/all
l'anno/ˈan.no/year

fields.Name: usually the syllable before the last
fields.Says: In Italian, stress is lexical, meaning it is word-specific and partly unpredictable. Penultimate stress (primary stress on the second-to-last syllable) is also generally preferred.
fields.Examples:
as in
buongiorno/ˌbwɔnˈd͡ʒor.no/good day
parlare/parˈla.re/to talk
grazie/ˈɡrat.t͡sje/thank you

fields.Name: an earlier syllable, and nothing is written
fields.Says: This use of accents is generally mandatory only to indicate stress on a word-final vowel; elsewhere, accents are generally found only in dictionaries.
fields.Examples:
as in
essere/ˈɛs.se.re/to be
subito/ˈsu.bi.to/at once
la domenica/doˈme.ni.ka/Sunday

fields.Letters: à · è · é · ì · ò · ù
fields.Name: stress on the last vowel
fields.Says: The acute accent (´) may be used on ⟨é⟩ and ⟨ó⟩ to represent stressed close-mid vowels. This use of accents is generally mandatory only to indicate stress on a word-final vowel; elsewhere, accents are generally found only in dictionaries. […] The grave accent (`) is found on ⟨à⟩, ⟨è⟩, ⟨ì⟩, ⟨ò⟩, ⟨ù⟩.
fields.Examples:
as in
perché/perˈke/because
la città/t͡ʃitˈta/town
il lunedì/lu.neˈdi/Monday

fields.Name: words of one syllable
fields.Says: Monosyllabic words generally lack an accent (e.g. ho, me). The accent is written, however, if there is an ⟨i⟩ or a ⟨u⟩ preceding another vowel (più, può). This applies even if the ⟨i⟩ is "silent", i.e. part of the digraphs ⟨ci⟩ or ⟨gi⟩ representing /tʃ/ and /dʒ/ (ciò, giù). It does not apply, however, if the word begins with ⟨qu⟩ (qua, qui).
fields.Examples:
as in
più/ˈpju/more
già/ˈd͡ʒa/already
qui/ˈkwi/here

fields.Name: one-syllable words told apart by the accent
fields.Says: Many monosyllabic words are spelled with an accent in order to avoid ambiguity with other words (e.g. là, lì versus la, li). This is known as accento distintivo […].
fields.Examples:
as in
là/ˈla/there
lì/ˈli/there
lithem
